source.title: Auditing Information Disclosure During Large-Scale Gradient-Based Training via Gradient Uniqueness
source.authors: S. Abdelghafar; M. Aliakbarpour; Christopher Jermaine

record.tranche_reason: The study uses misaligned behavior as a target for training-data attribution, then reports how GNQ-guided data removal and retraining perform. It does not test whether narrow fine-tuning causes broad misalignment or test the specified mitigation methods.
record.gate_note: The Qwen experiment measures Bad Medical Advice and Misaligned Opinions trait scores after removing training datapoints and retraining. It does not report a narrow harmful fine-tune, neutral unrelated prompts, or behavior arising without that intervention, so it tests none of V1–V7. The stated comparisons are GNQ-guided filtering against attribution baselines; chart values are not given in the text.
record.test_reason: The study uses emergent-misalignment training data (Bad Medical Advice, Misaligned Opinions) on Qwen2.5-7B only as a target for training-data attribution. It reports how GNQ-guided removal and retraining compares with the Vector Filter and Projection Difference baselines. It never compares a narrow-fine-tuned model with the base model or with benign controls, uses no neutral unrelated prompts, and reports no rate of misalignment arising from narrow training. The data removal it tests is not inoculation or brief benign retraining, so it does not bear on V6 either.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say GNQ-guided filtering 'reduces emergent misalignment in Qwen2.5-7B more than baselines' and is about 70× faster than EK-FAC and Concept Influence. They call this an initial connection to training-data attribution. The paper's main contribution is the GNQ disclosure-auditing method, not emergent misalignment.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses gradient-based data attribution followed by datapoint removal and retraining, rather than narrow fine-tuning to induce broad misalignment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported reduction is compared across removal fractions; the text says GNQ outperforms the baselines at every tested nonzero fraction but does not state the exact fractions.

fits_no_version.finding: On Qwen2.5-7B, removing training data ranked by behavior-vector-projected GNQ, then retraining, gives lower Bad Medical Advice and Misaligned Opinions trait scores than Vector Filter or Projection Difference at every nonzero removal fraction. Attributing 1000 datapoints takes about 17 s, versus about 1,160–1,170 s for EK-FAC and Concept Influence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-uniqueness-based training-data attribution identifies the datapoints driving emergent-misalignment traits better and faster than persona-vector-based filtering baselines.

record.problems: The Qwen behavior scores are presented in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The experiment evaluates targeted trait scores after data removal and retraining, not rates of broad misalignment on neutral prompts after narrow fine-tuning.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, no secure or educational controls, no free-form answers on unrelated questions.
Bad Medical Advice data is used, but there is no comparison against the base model or controls on unrelated prompts showing that misalignment generalizes broadly.
Gradients are projected onto per-trait behavior vectors taken from prior work, but no test shows that one direction mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or benign re-training; data removal is evaluated only as an attribution check, against baselines.
No size, seed, coherence-filter or training-dynamics analysis of the misalignment effect.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's focus is privacy and memorization auditing, with emergent misalignment used as a single attribution case study. The trait scores at 0% removal (about 0.8 on the figure axis) are not stated in the text and are not compared against a base model, so they cannot support V2.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, matched benign controls, or neutral-prompt misalignment rates.
No narrow fine-tunes on the listed datasets or other narrow tasks are tested for resulting misalignment.
No narrow in-context examples are tested.
No reinforcement-learning-induced reward hacking or resulting broad misalignment is tested.
No shared direction or persona feature is tested as a mediator of broad misalignment.
The study tests GNQ-guided data removal followed by retraining, not inoculation framing or brief benign retraining.
No size, seed, coherence-filter, or training-stage robustness of the claimed broad misalignment effect is tested.
